To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the rate of phenotypical evolution is correlated with the importance of the trait to fitness; (ii) this correlation is consistent with adaptation, in contrast to the neutral theory; (iii) this correlation is not found for gene expression traits.
the rate of evolution of a phenotypic trait is correlated with the importance of the trait to fitness, and that morphological traits are more likely to evolve adaptively than gene expression traits.
(1) yeast morphological evolution has been adaptive and (2) the neutral hypothesis of evolution cannot explain all aspects of the phenotypic evolution of yeast.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of morphological traits in yeast.
the evolution of yeast morphology and gene expression, and we are particularly interested in understanding the relative contributions of adaptation and neutral evolution to these phenotypic traits.
the evolution of yeast morphological traits and their underlying genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neutral theory of phenotypic variation is false.
the neutral hypothesis of morphological evolution has been falsified in yeast.
neutral evolution is not a universal phenomenon for phenotypic evolution, but that its importance varies among phenotypes and species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neutral hypothesis of evolution holds for the majority of phenotypic traits, and is thus the null hypothesis for phenotypic evolution studies.
the neutral theory of evolution is not applicable to all aspects of biology.
the neutral theory of phenotypic (and molecular) evolution is not rejected by the data, but it is also not supported.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of adaptation, the rate of evolution of a trait should be inversely proportional to the importance of the trait to fitness.
, contrary to common wisdom, neutral evolution may not be a dominant force in phenotypic evolution, at least in yeast.
the neutral theory of phenotypic variation is not a priori valid and should be tested on a trait-by-trait basis, as is done for molecular evolution.
